prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling through ligand design and mechanistic understanding

statement.case_for: I have moved from B002 to B052 as my preferred single-part prize. The reason is the test I set the committee in round 1: separate the original discovery from later refinement and be able to say exactly who did what. For B052 the file supports an answer. Buchwald and Hartwig independently built general, ligand-controlled catalysts in the mid-1990s and then established the mechanism (oxidative addition, amine binding, reductive elimination) that let the ligands be designed rather than found by screening. That is a principle plus quantitative mechanistic evidence plus three decades of independent confirmation and daily use in drug and materials synthesis, which is the combination I look for. It is the only candidate with explicit support from four members across subfields, and the two-name citation can be explained to a broad audience without leaving anyone obvious out. In round 1 I treated the attribution clarity of B052 as a point against my own choice; after reading the full exchange I think it is the decisive point in its favour.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised by Aqvist, Somfai and Zou, is that this extends the cross-coupling prize of 2010 to a new bond type and may read as a sequel rather than a new concept. I think the ligand-design and mechanism work answers that, but a physicist's instinct for a new organising principle still pulls toward condensates, and I cannot call the matter closed. Kosugi's tin-amide coupling is a genuine precursor, and no file settles his priority beyond the statements that his reaction was narrow and not ligand-controlled. A citation that stresses generality and ligand design is the honest way to draw that line, and the committee should say so in the expert report. Hartwig and Buchwald also appear elsewhere in the candidate pool, so the names could be credited under more than one ballot ID.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks C-N coupling first as a game-changer with a clean Buchwald-Hartwig attribution, and flags Kosugi and Migita-type precursors as a priority question he cannot settle from the files.
responses.response: I now agree with Johan on the configuration and on the clean two-person attribution. On the open question that he and the chair's summary both raise, my reading is that the discriminating criterion is generality under ligand control. A stoichiometric tin-amide reaction that works for a narrow range of substrates is a precursor, not the discovery of a general catalytic method, and the citation wording should say 'general' and 'ligand design' so that Kosugi is outside it by construction. I do not claim the files prove this; it is a judgment the expert report must document, and I would ask Johan whether he would accept that wording as sufficient.

responses.point: Somfai prefers B052 alone, argues the C-N bond was left unrecognised in 2010 and that the ligand and mechanistic work was new chemistry, and worries that omitting Kosugi invites a priority argument.
responses.response: Peter's synthetic perspective is what moved me most, in particular the point that the three decades of bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphine development are real chemistry and not scope extension. I asked him in round 1 to separate the original general discovery from refinements, and his answer, that the mid-1990s general catalysts plus mechanistic work are the discovery and the later ligand generations are refinement, is the separation I wanted. I would ask him to say which of the later ligand generations he considers part of the credited achievement, since that determines whether the citation should name ligand design at all.

responses.point: Sparr holds B002 as a new thermodynamic concept of cell organisation, and says physical chemistry has had little recognition compared with synthesis.
responses.response: Emma and I held the same configuration in round 1 and I take her argument about physical chemistry seriously; it is the main thing that keeps B002 as my first alternative. Where I have moved is on what the file can bear: with three names the set Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen omits Pappu and Mittag, whose sticker-spacer theory is the quantitative principle I valued, and she herself says that claims of generality are probably overstated. A prize whose central physical principle is credited to people outside the citation, and whose physiological relevance both of us call disputed, is less defensible today than one with a settled attribution. I would regard it as a strong candidate in a later year if the in vivo evidence matures.

responses.point: Zou argues B052 is the only candidate with broad cross-subfield support and a stable attribution, notes that Kosugi's reaction was not general or ligand-controlled, and flags that his 1994-1995 timeline relies on recollection.
responses.response: Xiaodong's statement that Kosugi's reaction was neither general nor ligand-controlled is the claim on which the exclusion rests, and he correctly flags that his dates are from memory. I therefore treat it as a lead for the expert report to verify against the original papers, not as an established fact. If the primary literature confirms the 1994-1995 timeline and the scope limits, the case for a two-name citation is strong; if it shows meaningful generality in the earlier work, I would want the committee to reopen the question rather than rely on our recollections.

responses.point: Aili proposes a two-part prize pairing C-N coupling (Buchwald, Hartwig) with base editing (Liu alone) for balance between a synthetic method and a biomolecular tool.
responses.response: This answers the chair's question about a second part, and I considered it. I do not prefer it because balance across subfields is not itself a scientific reason, and it forces Liu alone into a part whose attribution (Komor and Gaudelli, and the independent Kondo and Nishida work) is contested and which sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize. Daniel and Andrei both say the long-term safety record is still emerging, and I give that weight. B004 is therefore my second alternative, and I would return to it if the committee is split and needs a second part.

uncertainties: Whether Kosugi's tin-amide coupling was general and ligand-controlled enough to share the credit; this has to be settled from the original papers and not from recollection.
Whether the committee will see B052 as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether the physiological relevance of condensates will be settled soon enough to make B002 competitive in a coming year.
Whether a physicist's preference for a new organising principle is biasing me against a method whose impact is large but whose concept is incremental.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile with any shortlisted candidate. I am a physicist at Lund University and my Lund colleagues Somfai and Sparr are on the committee, but none of the shortlisted candidates is a Lund collaborator in my profile. Changing my preferred position is the result of the exchange and not of any relationship. As chair I disclosed in round 1 that I supported B002 and I now no longer do.
